title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Ethics - Biotechnology - Proper citation formats
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: When formatting a bibliography entry for a primary research article in standard scientific formats (such as Council of Science Editors (CSE) or APA), which piece of information is critical for unambiguously identifying the specific digital location of the article so future readers can retrieve it?
options: The corresponding author's institutional email address
The federal grant number that funded the research
The total number of citations the paper has received
questions.explain:
The **Digital Object Identifier (DOI)** is a unique alphanumeric string assigned to a digital document (like a journal article) that provides a persistent link to its location on the internet. 

Unlike URLs, which can break or change, a DOI remains permanently tied to the document. It is a mandatory component in modern scientific citation formats to ensure readers can easily locate the source material.

questions.q: In the introduction of a molecular biology manuscript, the author writes: *"CRISPR-Cas9 mediated knockout of the p53 gene has been shown to accelerate tumor progression in murine models [4]."* What is the primary ethical and functional purpose of the bracketed number `[4]` in this sentence?
options: To indicate that the sentence is a direct, word-for-word quotation from the original author.
To signify that the journal has ranked this claim as the fourth most important finding of the decade.
To direct the reader to the corresponding entry in the bibliography, properly attributing the idea to its original discoverers.
To indicate the exact lab notebook page where the author recorded this observation.
questions.explain:
In scientific writing (which heavily uses numbered citation styles like IEEE, Nature, or AMA), a bracketed or superscript number in the text is an **in-text citation**. 

Its purpose is to provide immediate, traceable credit to the researchers who originally generated the data or concept, while directing the reader to the full reference details in the bibliography at the end of the document. Standard scientific writing rarely uses direct quotes (making Option 'a' incorrect), relying instead on paraphrased summaries with citation.

questions.q: A student copies a dense paragraph detailing the chemical mechanism of DNA polymerase directly from a textbook into their laboratory report. To avoid plagiarizing, the student changes three or four verbs to synonyms, leaves the sentence structure intact, and places a standard citation at the end of the paragraph. According to academic integrity standards, why is this practice still considered a form of plagiarism?
options: The student committed "patchwriting" (mosaic plagiarism) by failing to synthesize and significantly restructure the original author's words.
Textbooks are classified as tertiary sources and therefore cannot be legally cited in an academic document.
The student failed to bold the replaced synonyms to indicate they had altered the text.
DNA replication mechanisms are patented, requiring legal permission rather than a simple citation.
questions.explain:
Replacing just a few words with synonyms while maintaining the original sentence structure is known as **patchwriting or mosaic plagiarism**. 

Even if a citation is provided at the end, presenting another author's exact phrasing (or heavily mimicking it) as your own writing is considered plagiarism in the scientific community. To paraphrase correctly, a writer must completely synthesize the information and rewrite it in their own distinct sentence structure and voice.
